newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr breaks losing streak, high on yen.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr breaks losing streak, high on yen.

text.p: The Australian dollar held onto 1/2 cent of offshore gains through a choppy session Wednesday, breaking a four-day losing streak and establishing a short term uptrend for the recently beleagured currency.

Traders said aggressive buying from a U.S. investment bank and hurried short covering had fuelled the rally which saw the currency touch US$0.7825 at once stage before attracting sustained profit-taking from U.S. funds.
A continued selloff in the low yielding yen and European currencies underpined the relatively high paying dollar and briefly saw it to a five year high on the Japanese unit.
By 5.00 am (0700 GMT) the dollar had found a foothold at US$0.7810/15 from an early US$0.7805/10 and US$0.7772/77 late here Tuesday.
Analysts said a break past here would suggest Tuesday's six-week low of US$0.7735 had marked a floor in the currency's month-old downtrend and a recovery toward 79 cents was likley.
Dealers said it had been aided by talk another Victorian power station was being sold to an offshore group which rumour said would result in demand for some A$1.5 billion of dollars.
Some were sceptical of the amount, however, saying the latest information was it would only be around A$200 million.

On the crosses it gained on the yen after the Bank of Japan had reaffirmed its relaxed policy stance with an accomodative money market operation this morning which pushed money rates below the official 0.50 percent.

The Ministry of Finance later chimed in saying Japan would maintain its easy credit policy, leaving dealers confident in their expectations of further Japanese investment in higher yielding currencies like the U.S. and local dollars.
The currency duly climbed to a five year high of 99.08/18 yen, way up on Tuesday's late 97.75/85 while the U.S. dollar rushed to a 56-month peak of 126.93 yen.
The latest rise brought the dollar's gains this year to eight yen or 8.6 percent and meant it had appreciated by no less than 69 percent since troughing around 59.00 yen in May 1995.

Investors were also pulling funds out of low yielding European currencies, encouraged by renewed confidence in the process of European Monetary Union which diminished the attractiveness of safe havens like the mark and Swiss franc.
The local dollar made it to 1.3400/13 marks from 1.3302/15 late Tuesday and to 60.6 in trade weighted terms from 60.1.
The Wallis report on reform of the financial system proved something of an anti-climax as far as the market was concerned.

The report did recommend a relaxation of takeover rules for banks and other financial institutions, but Treasurer Peter Costello said the government would not allow any of the four major Australian banks to merge.
There had been speculation at least two of the banks would have merged if allowed with a resulting shakeout in the forex industry here.

Costello did remove the ban on offshore banks bidding for domestic ones, a potential positive for the A$, but emphasised that large scale foreign takeover of the banking system would be against the national interest.
Such a bid could also have indirect implications for the dollar since even the most vulnerable, ANZ and Westpac, were worth around A$ 12 billion, implying a similar demand for the currency.
Elsewhere, analysts were looking forward to the first and only significant piece of domestic data this week in the shape of the March unemployment report on Thursday.
Expectations are for a 13,500 rise in employment, reversing a 7,200 drop in February, and a dip in the jobless rate to 8.7 percent from 8.8.
